Metric construction and evaluation are not cleanly separated. Components, combinations, prompts, and design variants are examined using the same 1,000 human-rated pairs on which the headline performance is reported, with no held-out development/test split. The only independent check has just 50 pairs, lacks significance tests, and changes Object F1's vocabulary to the dataset's 50 test classes.

The central use case—ranking brain-decoding systems—is not validated against human judgments. The main meta-evaluation concerns pair-level scores from one decoder, while the five-model table provides neither human model-level rankings nor uncertainty, matched sampling details, or evidence that SEED selects the better system.

The statistical analysis has serious weaknesses. Bootstrapping only evaluators treats the 1,000 images as fixed and cannot support generalization to new stimuli; a crossed or hierarchical bootstrap over both raters and images is needed. Reported numbers are also inconsistent: Cap-Sim's Pearson correlation is .666 in Table 1 but .683 in Table 5, and the reported Kendall improvement confidence interval [.02, .04] does not contain the tabulated point improvement of .062.

Important metric choices are arbitrary or underspecified: raw components with different ranges and distributions are equally averaged; sensitivity to scaling and weights is not tested; Object F1 is restricted to a COCO-centric vocabulary; empty-detection cases are undefined; and exact checkpoints, feature layers, preprocessing, caption decoding, and text-embedding model are not specified.

The robustness and failure-mode evidence is weaker than claimed. Figure 3 aggregates eight model combinations without reporting their individual results, while the near-miss threshold and semantic-detail-miss criterion are arbitrary. The latter is partly circular because it defines failure using a difference involving SEED itself and is not validated by human annotation.

Reproducibility is currently poor: the manuscript twice says code and human data are 'available at' but supplies no URL. The human-study protocol also omits randomization, attention checks, exclusions, completion time, rater composition, and ethics/consent information; the adequacy of the stated $0.03 payment per two judgments therefore cannot be assessed.
